claims.claim: In visual analysis, a line can be described as an identifiable path that varies in width, direction, and length.

Lines can define the edges of forms and can guide attention through a composition; their observable qualities include whether they are horizontal, vertical, diagonal, straight, curved, thick, or thin.
A contour line defines the boundary of a shape or figure, while closely spaced hatching can create shading and help suggest form in a two-dimensional image.

Line is one formal feature among several that can be examined in close visual analysis; an interpretation should connect a claim to visible evidence and not treat formal observation alone as proof of intention or fixed meaning.
Terms such as horizontal, vertical, diagonal, continuous, broken, thick, thin, straight, and curved describe observable qualities rather than universal emotional messages.
A visual-analysis claim can be qualified: repeated diagonals may guide attention toward an area, but that observation by itself does not establish why a maker chose them or how every viewer responds.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Introductory resources sometimes attach suggested moods to line directions, while visual effects depend on the surrounding work, medium, audience, and context.
positions: Museum learning resources use direction and character to prompt discussion of possible effects such as movement or repose.
Formal analysis treats line as evidence to interpret in a specific composition, rather than as a one-to-one code for emotion or intention.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson asks students to name observable line qualities and make qualified, work-specific claims. It does not present any line direction or character as carrying one universal mood or meaning.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft gave no art-specific definition of line, no account of contour or hatching, and no way to distinguish observation from interpretation.
The draft's generic vocabulary and three-option checks did not meet the lesson or assessment requirements.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic study-skills prose with source-verified definitions and uses of line in formal analysis.
Added the distinction between contour and hatching, and between visible evidence and claims about meaning or intention.
Created an original worked example and five four-option questions spanning recall, understanding, application, and analysis.
rightsIssues: Getty, Smarthistory, and the National Gallery of Art resources are used as reference-only sources. No source prose, images, or teaching materials are reproduced or adapted.
